title: Continents drift about as fast as your fingernails grow
body: Earth’s rigid outer shell is broken into tectonic plates that glide over the hot, slowly deforming mantle beneath. At the Mid-Atlantic Ridge they spread apart by roughly 1 to 4 cm a year, about as fast as [fingernails grow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nail_%28anatomy%29) (about 3.5 mm a month), while the Pacific’s Nazca Plate moves up to about 16 cm a year. Tiny as that sounds, over [roughly 200 million years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangaea) such motion tore apart the supercontinent Pangaea and opened the whole Atlantic Ocean.

slides.question: How far does the Pacific’s Nazca Plate move in a year, at most?
slides.explanation: Up to about 16 cm a year, against roughly 1 to 4 cm at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Over about 200 million years, such motion tore Pangaea apart and opened the Atlantic.

slides.alt: Animation on a survey map: a fingernail and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge creep along one ruler for a year (42 mm against 10 to 40 mm), the Nazca Plate reaches 160 mm, then a simplified Atlantic opens between two continent outlines and a cross-section shows the ridge.

slides.heading: How far they move in a year
slides.note: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge spreads 10–40 mm a year; fingernails grow about 3.5 mm a month.

slides.clue: The supercontinent whose slow break-up opened the Atlantic Ocean
slides.detail: From the Greek for ‘all the Earth’. Its break-up is still under way: the Atlantic widens a few centimetres a year.
